cards.title: Incremental change detection with an anti-join
questions: how do you detect new records when the source has no change feed
how does the proposal pipeline know which documents are new
anti-join change detection
how do you do incremental loads without cdc
why compute the delta in python instead of a database link
why not use a dblink between the two oracle databases
what happens when there are no new documents
how does she find only the net-new attachments
incremental processing of only new ids
delta as the work queue

how do you avoid reprocessing the whole corpus every night
how do you find records that haven't been processed yet

cards.answer: When a source gives me no change feed, I compute the delta myself and make the delta the work queue. For research proposals, the pipeline queries Kuali for every current proposal and award attachment ID, queries the destination tables for IDs already processed, and anti-joins the two sets in Python. Only net-new document IDs move on to BLOB retrieval. I chose that over a database link because the two Oracle databases sit in different security zones, and a cross-zone dblink is operationally expensive and policy-sensitive. Diffing in Python keeps the boundary intact and lets the pipeline run from anywhere with credentials to both sides. An empty delta is a normal outcome: the stage logs SUCCESS and exits cleanly, so the monitor doesn't mistake a quiet day for a failure. The limit is that an ID anti-join sees new records, not edits; where content changes matter, as with legislation, I compare content hashes instead.

cards.title: Rollback SQL and post-write verification on database writes
questions: what does the auto generated rollback sql look like
how do you verify rows were actually written to the database
post-write row count verification
how do you undo a bad write to a production table
how is the writeback to oracle made safe to rerun
insert where not exists or merge
how do you guard a truncate in production
what happens if fewer rows land than you attempted
how does she make database writes reversible
rollback plan for a pipeline write
dry run and confirm production flags
how do you make writeback idempotent
cards.answer: I make a write safe to repeat and cheap to undo before I worry about anything else. In the research proposals pipeline every insert into the Oracle staging tables is INSERT WHERE NOT EXISTS or a MERGE, so re-running an already processed batch is a no-op. After each write the pipeline queries the destination database and compares the confirmed row count with the count it attempted; a shortfall raises a RuntimeError inside the run, not in a dashboard a week later. Every run prints its rollback SQL to the log: DELETE statements carrying the exact FILE_DATA_ID list and an UPDATE_TIMESTAMP filter, so recovery doesn't require reading code. The one operation that can't be idempotent, the production TRUNCATE, is double-gated behind dry_run=False and confirm_production=True, both set explicitly. That's a little ceremony per run, and it's cheap next to a half-written table.

cards.title: Point-in-time extraction from the data warehouse
questions: how do you build a historical training set from mutable warehouse tables
effective dated reads
point in time snapshots from the edw
how did you build the retirement training panel
as of date extraction from hr tables
why not read the current row for historical examples
anchor dates and label windows
what is anchor safety
how does she avoid corrupting history with current data
person year panel construction
time based train test split on panel data
warehouse data definition problems you found
how do you keep current records from leaking into historical training rows
what check aborts the run when the training panel looks broken
cards.answer: If source rows are mutable, I read them as of the date I'm modeling, never as of today. Rebuilding the retirement risk forecast, I built a training panel the original never had: annual point-in-time snapshots from 2005 onward, each anchor capturing exactly who was active that day and labeling them forward twelve months. That came to 4,891 person-year rows across 622 people at a 2.4% base rate. Every anchor uses strict effective-dated reads; current rows read as of today would have corrupted every historical example while looking correct. The last usable anchor sits twelve months before the run date, so a missing retirement is a true negative, not an unfinished window. Splits are by anchor year only. SQL lives in version-controlled files with shared cohort CTEs, and the run aborts if the panel returns fewer than 30 positives. I also logged a defect for the warehouse team: two incompatible service-year definitions.

cards.title: Design: incremental loads from a rate-limited API
questions: how would you design incremental loads from an api with rate limits
how do you handle api rate limits in ingestion
what do you do when an api returns 429
polite polling design

per host backoff
how do you avoid hammering a source

backoff that froze the loop
designing an api ingestion job that respects quotas
throttling and retry design for api pulls
how would you schedule a daily pull against an api with request caps
how do you keep a poller or scraper from being blocked by a site
cards.answer: I'd let the cheapest possible call decide whether any expensive call happens. On the legislative pipeline that's one LegiScan hash check per run, then downloads only for sessions whose hash changed: 2 to 4 calls on a normal day instead of a full pull. Second, politeness belongs in the client, not in each caller. In my personal Drop Radar project, which polls about 40 sources, each source has its own interval, hosts are spaced, and a 403 or 429 triggers per-host backoff. A bug taught me the third rule: back off by skipping the blocked host, never by sleeping, because a sleeping backoff froze the whole loop for up to an hour. Fourth, persist the hash or cursor only after the data has landed, so a failed run retries rather than skips. On a shared LLM server I also rate-limited calls and gated the full run behind a five-case sanity check.

cards.title: Manifest design: one row per path, pointers and derived fields
questions: walk me through the rims manifest schema
why one row per file path instead of one row per unique file
why keep embeddings and text out of the manifest
how wide is the manifest
why is the layer field derived
partitioned parquet manifest
what does null mean in a stage status column
how do you make the work queue a query
what bugs did schema testing find
nan is truthy bug
dataframe fragmentation from adding columns one at a time
how did she design the archival pipeline manifest
why keep vectors and text as references outside the table
how does a stage know which files are still waiting for it
the central table every stage reads and writes
cards.answer: The RIMS manifest is one row per file path, 116 columns, written as partitioned Parquet, and a few choices in it do most of the work. One row per path, never collapsed: a file in three places is three archival facts, so deduplication is recorded in duplicate_of and duplicate_count instead of deleting rows. Per-stage status columns are null until that stage runs, so the queue is a query (WHERE s03_status IS NULL) and 'not reached' differs from 'found nothing'. Extracted text and embeddings live outside as pointers, because 384-dimension vectors at five million rows is about 7.5 GB in a column almost nothing reads. The layer field is recomputed from decision columns, never typed in, so it can't drift. Schema testing caught two bugs I kept as teaching examples: NaN is truthy, which put every row in layer 0, and adding a hundred columns one at a time fragments a DataFrame.

cards.title: File identity, deduplication and quarantine instead of delete
questions: how do you deduplicate files in an archive
blake2b file uid
content addressing in your pipeline
why quarantine instead of deleting files
nsrl known file filtering
what files get filtered before anything expensive runs
how do you make re-crawls produce stable ids
free filter tier
how much does the filter tier remove
how does she handle duplicate files without losing provenance
zero byte files lock files and thumbs.db
exact duplicate detection by hash
do you delete files the pipeline excludes
skipping system files and known software before processing
cards.answer: I separate identity from content, and I record deduplication as a decision rather than a deletion. Each manifest row gets a deterministic file_uid, a blake2b hash over the source identifier plus the normalized path, so re-crawling an accession yields identical keys and successive manifest generations join cleanly. Content duplicates are found by hash, but the rows stay and carry duplicate_of and duplicate_count. The free-filter tier drops NSRL known files, zero-byte files, lock files, .DS_Store and Thumbs.db, caches, node_modules and .git internals before anything expensive runs. Exclusion is written into the manifest, never applied as a removal, so every disposal is auditable and reversible, which is what retention obligations require. The 40 to 70% reduction from that tier is a working estimate in an explicit assumptions table, and I required it to be measured on a complete drive before anyone sizes hardware on it.

cards.title: Format identification: adopting preservation tools instead of rebuilding them
questions: how do you identify file formats

apache tika exiftool docling evaluation

archivematica and preservica
how does she decide between existing tools and custom code in the archive pipeline
forensic disk imaging

cards.answer: My default is to plug proven preservation software into the pipeline rather than write a first-pass layer myself. For the RIMS build I directed a structured evaluation of Siegfried and DROID for PRONOM format identification, BitCurator for write-blocked forensic acquisition and disk imaging, ExifTool, Apache Tika, Docling, the NSRL Reference Data Set, ePADD, Preservica and Archivematica, scored against a rubric. The deliverable was a recommendation: what to adopt, what to skip, and what genuinely remains to be written. The reasoning is maintenance. If professional software sits behind an adapter, its updates arrive for free, and where the university already holds a license we use it. The stage boundary makes that possible: stage 01 takes a root path and walks it, whether it's a mounted drive, an SMB share, a forensic image or a Box folder. Facts in a file header are read, never inferred by a model.

cards.title: Text extraction across 15+ file types
questions: how do you extract text from many different file types
15 file types extraction
legacy doc xls ppt extraction

cards.answer: I route every file to an extractor by type and make sure nothing is silently dropped. The legacy file archive covered 15+ types: PyPDF2 for PDFs, python-docx for .docx, BeautifulSoup for HTML, striprtf for RTF, zipfile for archives, a local vision model for images, and column structure for spreadsheets. Corrupted and custom-extension files fell back to filename cleanup, extension inference and folder-level summarization. The weak point was legacy Office: .doc, .xls and .ppt went through Win32 COM automation, which can't run on Colab or the Linux GPU server, can't be parallelized safely, and hangs on malformed files. So for the unified pipeline, porting that path to Apache Tika plus headless LibreOffice is a prerequisite rather than cleanup, with output parity checked against the proof of concept on the same files. Every extraction loop checkpoints per batch and resumes without redoing finished files.

cards.title: Handling bad records without dropping them
questions: what do you do with records that fail to parse
do you drop bad rows
how do you handle misnamed files
magic byte validation
rejection bucket with reason codes
documents with too little text
how do you handle null blobs
poison pill record
what happens when one record fails every night
how does she deal with malformed input
dead letter handling in a batch pipeline

where do unprocessable records end up
a corrupt input fails the job every night
cards.answer: A bad record should become a counted, labeled row, not an exception that kills the batch or a row that quietly disappears. In the research proposals pipeline a four-byte magic-number check catches DOCX files misnamed as .pdf, and they go to a rejection bucket with a reason code. Null BLOBs are counted against the expected total and logged as warnings. Documents with fewer than 40 valid words after cleaning are marked SUCCESSFULLY_PARSED=N and still flow to the output beside the parsed ones. The monitor applies the same rule to itself: an unreadable log becomes a synthetic LOG_READ_FAILED record that can alert. The opposite failure needs a guard too. One malformed bill failed, was never written, reappeared as a delta and failed again for six days; the remedy I specified is a length guard plus a retry ceiling that parks it. That's a dead-letter queue by another name.

cards.title: Email ingestion at scale, and what I'd change
questions: how did you ingest 44,677 email files

cards.answer: The email archive was a parsing problem first and an AI problem second. A 20-year PST export became 44,677 .eml files with readpst, keeping the folder hierarchy. I walked the tree with os.walk, parsed single-part and multipart MIME with Python's email library, kept text/plain parts with a UTF-8 fallback, and stored the folder path as queryable Folder_N columns. Splitting threads on the Original Message delimiter exploded the files into 79,676 message rows, and regex header extraction gave each From, Sent, To, Cc and Subject. Output was written in batches to CSV, resuming from the existing row count. What I'd change: summarization ran at about 34.78 seconds per email because the Ollama CLI reloaded the model on every call, so 100,000 rows projected to roughly 40 days. I'd serve the model persistently over HTTP and key resume on a row ID hash rather than a row count.

cards.title: The logging contract behind pipeline monitoring
questions: what columns are in your pipeline log schema
explain the logging contract
pipeline_start and pipeline_end sentinel rows
why do all pipelines log the same schema
what is upstream_failed
run id shared across stages
how do you onboard a new pipeline to monitoring
structured parquet logs
what does a pipeline log row contain
how does she standardize pipeline logging
logging when a process is killed mid run
log schema design for etl
how do you tell the root failure from stages skipped because of it
how do you know a run started but never finished
cards.answer: Centralized monitoring only works if every pipeline logs the same way, so the log schema is a contract. Each pipeline writes a Parquet log with workflow_name, a run_id shared by every stage of one execution, script_name and script_order, a status (SUCCESS, FAILED, UPSTREAM_FAILED, PIPELINE_START, PIPELINE_END), an is_success flag, UTC event times and durations, and on failure the error type, message, traceback and failure stage. The START and END sentinel rows make silence detectable: a run with a start and no end is incomplete. UPSTREAM_FAILED separates the root cause from the cascade it caused, so one failure doesn't read as five. The retirement pipeline rewrites its log after every event, so a process killed mid-run still records the attempt. Onboarding a new pipeline is one path added to a config list, with no new monitor code.

cards.title: Silence thresholds and alert severity tiers
questions: how do you decide which pipeline failures send an alert
severity tiers critical warning info
silence threshold for pipelines
48 hour silence rule
2400 hour threshold for quarterly jobs
how do you avoid alert fatigue
how does the monitor detect a missed run
why sendmail instead of smtp

per pipeline silence override

how do you notice a job that never ran
stopping a quarterly job from alerting constantly

cards.answer: Alerts are tiered by status and age so only actionable failures interrupt anyone. CRITICAL is a FAILED or LOG_READ_FAILED record in the last 24 hours, WARNING is a failure within 7 days, INFO is anything older plus UPSTREAM_FAILED cascade rows. Only CRITICAL sends email, but that email carries the WARNING and INFO rows as context. Silence is detected separately from failure: the monitor computes hours since each pipeline's last successful run and flags any past its threshold. The standard is 48 hours. A quarterly pipeline would breach that two days after every run and then alert for 89 days, so the retirement pipeline has a per-pipeline override of 2,400 hours, with matching Grafana targets. Mail goes through the server's local sendmail, because outbound SMTP isn't available there. The monitor itself runs on cron every 30 to 60 minutes.

cards.title: Auditing the monitor: drift, rosters and unverified alerts
questions: have you audited your own monitoring
monitoring configuration drift
how do you know your alerts are actually delivered

what was wrong with the health check

what did the july 2026 reliability audit find
how does she check the monitoring itself
alerting that never sent
monitor thresholds never imported
what did reviewing your health checks turn up
cards.answer: A monitor is a pipeline too, so I audit it like one. My July 2026 audit of the legislative pipeline found four things. Stages emitted a success record while producing zero output, so a failing job reported green; the fix I specified makes completion require a non-zero output count. The roster was inferred from whatever happened to log, and the two most broken stages weren't in it; it should be declared. Configuration had drifted: a documented 6 AM schedule for a job that ran at 4 AM, thresholds defined but never imported. And delivery was never verified: the code handed mail to the transport without checking the return value, and sender and recipient domains differed, so a month of 'alerts sent' could have been alerts never delivered. In my Drop Radar personal project, a watcher raises an alarm when no source has been checked for 30 minutes; it fired 34 minutes into a real outage.

cards.title: Scheduling choices: cron, JupyterHub Scheduler and timer Functions, not Airflow
questions: why didn't you use airflow
why cron instead of an orchestrator
how are your pipelines scheduled
jupyterhub scheduler for production
timer triggered azure functions
how do you handle dependencies between pipeline stages
when would you adopt a dag orchestrator
why build monitoring instead of adopting airflow
what scheduler runs the quarterly report
how does she orchestrate pipelines
decoupling jobs so one failure doesn't take down another
orchestration trade-offs
cards.answer: I matched each scheduler to where the job runs and put the real investment into knowing whether jobs did their work. The proposals pipeline and the monitor run on cron; the retirement report runs on cron at 06:00 on the first day of each quarter; the daily legislative rescore runs on the JupyterHub Scheduler at 4 AM; weekly digests and nightly impact scoring are timer-triggered Azure Functions. I haven't run Airflow in production. As the one person productionalizing that server, the gap I felt was observability, so I built the alerting and run-tracking layer myself. Dependencies inside a pipeline are explicit stages under one logger, with cascade status, and I decouple jobs that shouldn't share fate: the bill investigator is separate so it can't take down nightly scoring, and heavy jobs moved off JupyterHub after an out-of-memory failure. If cross-pipeline dependencies multiplied, a DAG orchestrator is where I'd go.

cards.title: Batch versus streaming ingestion
questions: batch or streaming ingestion
when would you use streaming instead of batch
have you built real time ingestion

does she build streaming pipelines
polling intervals per source

cards.answer: I pick the cadence from when the data stops being useful. Almost all my institutional work is batch: research proposals run on a schedule where 'nothing new' is a valid outcome, the legislative rescore runs daily, and the retirement report runs quarterly. Bills move over days and that report is read quarterly, so seconds buy nothing. My personal Drop Radar project is the opposite case: limited releases sell out in minutes, so it polls about 40 sources on per-source intervals that tighten inside known drop windows. Its Discord feed moved from 10-second REST polling to the official Gateway over a standard-library websocket with heartbeat, resume and dead-connection detection, so posts arrive in about a second, with polling as automatic fallback. An arrival log records each alert's upstream post, detection and send times. I haven't run Kafka or a managed streaming platform in production.

cards.title: Backfills, catch-up and reprocessing
questions: how do you run a backfill

cards.answer: A backfill should be one command and safe to kill. For the legislative corpus I built a single-command session backfill runner, so each additional General Assembly session is one invocation rather than a hand-staged chain; four full sessions went through every stage with all artifacts verified in Azure. The extractor flushes in batches and can be killed and restarted without double-writing, which an 11,673-bill run of roughly 155 hours requires, and each evaluation configuration wrote to its own isolated path so runs couldn't share state. When extraction silently stopped for 11 nights after a kernel update disabled the GPU driver, I protected the catch-up so no data was skipped. For routine reprocessing, nightly impact scoring keys on a content hash per bill, so only changed bills are re-evaluated, and the passage model trains on nine sessions while the application serves four.

cards.title: Design: ingesting and classifying millions of documents nightly
questions: how would you build a pipeline to ingest and classify millions of documents nightly
design a nightly document classification pipeline

cards.answer: I'd build it the way I designed the RIMS archival pipeline: cheap deterministic work first, expensive inference only on what survives. Inventory from metadata before downloading, as our Box ingest does with name, size, SHA-1, path and timestamps. A free-filter tier drops exact duplicates, NSRL known files and junk at zero cost. A manifest with one row per file and per-stage status columns makes each night's work queue a query and every run resumable. Classification runs on the survivors through a batching server: moving to vLLM continuous batching gave 6.22x on the same L4, taking 12,125 images from about 22 hours to 3.7. Writes stay idempotent, every stage logs to the shared contract, and silence alerts. The honest scale note: the unified system has run 2,375 real files in about 21 seconds on 4 vCPU; I haven't run millions nightly, and I'd measure the filter's reduction rate before sizing hardware.

cards.title: Design: making a pipeline restartable after a crash
questions: how would you make a pipeline restartable after a crash mid run
design for restart
what state do you persist so a job can resume
how do you resume without double writing
crash recovery for batch jobs
how do you avoid stale files from a previous run

checkpoint design
how would she design crash safe pipelines
what happens if the server reboots during a run
exactly once processing in batch
what has to be true so the next run just works after a failure

what do you store to resume a failed batch job
cards.answer: I design so a crash costs at most one batch and a restart needs no human decisions. Three mechanisms do most of it. State lives in the data: in the RIMS manifest a null stage status means not reached, so a restart queries for nulls, and 'processed, found nothing' isn't confused with 'never ran'. Work is flushed in batches and writes are idempotent: the legislative extractor can be killed and restarted without double-writing, and the proposal writes are WHERE NOT EXISTS or MERGE. And the log is rewritten after every event, so a killed process still records that it started. I clear temp directories at the start of each run so stale files can't contaminate the new one, and I cap retries so a poison record gets parked instead of failing forever. My early resumable CSVs resumed from a row count; I'd key resume on record ID hashes now, so a reordered input can't skip or repeat rows.

cards.title: Storage formats: Parquet, CSV or a database
questions: why parquet instead of csv
when do you write to a database instead of files
how do you choose a storage format
parquet versus csv versus database
how do you store lists and dicts in parquet
why did the prototype use json instead of the csvs
what format are your pipeline outputs

how does she choose file formats for pipelines
columnar storage choices
cards.answer: I choose storage by who reads it and how. Parquet is my default for intermediates, gold outputs and logs: typed, columnar and cheap to prune, which is why the nine session files and every pipeline log are Parquet. Writing it has a catch: lists and dicts must be normalized to JSON strings first, an explicit step in the proposals pipeline. CSV appeared in early prototypes where append-and-resume was the point, but text-heavy CSVs get big fast: 263 MB and 209 MB pipeline CSVs couldn't be parsed in a browser, so that prototype read a 5 MB pre-processed JSON. When analysts query results next to existing financial data, results belong in the database, so proposal output lands in Oracle staging tables. User state with expiry, like sessions and sign-in tokens, sits in Cosmos DB with TTL policies, and Blob Storage is the exchange layer between the server and the cloud app.

cards.answer: I want any output row traceable to its source without reading code. In the proposals pipeline, three staging tables let engineering follow a production row back through its NLP annotations to the original extracted text, and PDF metadata is saved to Parquet for audit. Every pipeline run carries a run_id shared across its stages. In the archive work, search results return the original Box path, the RIMS manifest keeps a deterministic blake2b file_uid, and reviewer decisions go to an append-only log where changing your mind adds an entry pointing at the first; 481 reviewer decisions came back stamped with the reviewer's name. In the legislative pipeline, raw model output sits beside each standardized field, the raw labeled action history is kept so the leakage guard can be re-derived, and evaluated model versions were pinned by blob digest, because re-pulling 'latest' fetches a moved tag.

cards.title: Cost and footprint of data pipelines
questions: how much do your pipelines cost to run

cards.answer: I put heavy batch work on hardware the institution already owns and pay for cloud only where latency needs it. The proposals NLP runs entirely on the Linux server with no external API calls, so there's no per-document cost. On the legislative platform, bulk inference runs on the on-premises GPU at no marginal cost while managed cloud inference handles low-latency requests in the app. Before asking for hardware I measure: moving to vLLM recovered 6.22x throughput on the same L4, and right-sizing the language model's GPU allocation freed about 15 GB so the archival pipeline could share the server. Where cloud is the answer, I size from the workload: a written Basic versus Premium v3 analysis for a memory-bound app, and an estimated $77 a month for the procurement deployment design. The unified archival system processed 2,375 files in about 21 seconds on 4 vCPU.

cards.title: Metadata extraction and normalization to archival standards
questions: how do you extract file metadata

cards.answer: I extract metadata from the file before asking any model about it, and I map it to a standard the receiving system already speaks. For 12,125 archival images I built a metadata pipeline with tifffile, Pillow and iptcinfo3 pulling file-level, EXIF/TIFF and IPTC fields: filename, size, format, MIME type, dimensions, resolution, compression, object name, caption and keywords. Every output field maps to IPTC Core and Dublin Core, so records move into library cataloguing systems without transformation work. The RIMS build made that a standing rule: for facts already in a file header, a model is used only to phrase them, never to discover them. Inventory metadata comes first as well. Box ingest builds the manifest from name, size, SHA-1, path and timestamps before a byte is downloaded. A metadata crosswalk is one of the open work items tracked in that build.

cards.title: Migrating a KNIME workflow into a production Python package
questions: how do you migrate knime workflows to python

cards.answer: I treat a KNIME migration as removing a single point of failure, not translating nodes. The retirement workflow was lost with its KNIME server, so the Python rebuild is a modular package: configuration, warehouse extraction, panel construction, report logic, writer, output-contract validation, age adjustment, structured logging and email delivery, under one entry point and a shell runner. Every SQL query moved into version-controlled files with shared cohort CTEs. A preflight script checks the Oracle client, credentials, imports, project files, distribution list and directory permissions before the first scheduled run, not at 6 AM on a quarter boundary. Each run validates against a frozen contract of 4 files, 21 sheets and 436 columns; a float equality check that passed at 224 rows and failed at 225 became a tolerance with a printed drift. Delivery failure raises. It runs quarterly on cron in about six minutes, registered with the monitor.

cards.title: Preparing six million catalog rows for matching
questions: how did you prepare the procurement data for matching
unifying vendor files into one schema
manufacturer name normalization
how did you clean six million catalog rows
blocked fuzzy clustering
llm canonicalization of names
multi vendor data preparation
converting vendor exports to parquet
how does she prep data for entity matching
schema mapping across distributors
the same manufacturer spelled many ways across vendors
getting supplier catalogs into a comparable shape
cards.answer: Before any matching, I made four vendors look like one table. The procurement work grew from a single 4 MB file, where I first cleaned encoding errors and phantom columns, to six files of about 1.1 GB across four distributors, converted to Parquet and mapped into one 12-column unified schema. Manufacturer names were normalized in three passes: programmatic cleanup took 3,205 names to 2,949, blocked fuzzy clustering with rapidfuzz grouped variants without comparing every pair, and an LLM canonicalized what remained, with a five-case sanity check gating the full run and rate-limited calls on the shared server. Then I checked field completeness before writing comparison logic, which is how the qsu pack-size field turned up. Only after that did exact manufacturer plus part-number matching run, confirming 42,052 identical products across 6,068,888 rows.

cards.title: Publishing per-session Parquet files to the gold layer
questions: how do you publish pipeline outputs to azure
overwrite safe upload of session parquets
why save the hash after the upload
what schema do the prediction parquets have
multi session parquet management
how does the app see the daily rescore
gold layer upload design
how do you know a session's artifacts are complete
how does she publish data to blob storage
overwrite versus append for outputs
cards.answer: The daily legislative run republishes nine per-session Parquet files to Azure gold, and the ordering is what makes that safe: hash check, conditional download, parse, label, rebuild history, rescore, build the active-bills snapshot, upload with overwrite, then save the hash. Because the hash is saved last, a run that fails before upload leaves the old hash in place and the next run reprocesses that session instead of skipping it. Whole-file overwrite keeps gold simple: each file is a complete replacement with a fixed schema (bill_id as Int64, bill_number, y_prob, n_actions, bill_year, momentum, generated_at). The app's one-hour cache TTL makes the 4 AM rescore visible the same day. A session only counted as done once gold features, Explorer metadata, FAISS index and config were verified present in Azure.

cards.title: Fitting NLP output into Oracle: the 11-step proposal chain
questions: walk me through the 11 step nlp chain
what are the 11 steps of the proposal nlp pipeline
why truncate keywords to 500 to 1000 characters
how do you store list columns in parquet
what is successfully_parsed
40 word minimum threshold
real word vocabulary cache
keybert batch size
how do you fit nlp output to database column limits
how does she shape nlp output for a relational table
what happens between loading proposal text and writing keywords to oracle
how are proposals turned into keywords step by step
cards.answer: The 11-step chain in the proposals pipeline is as much data engineering as NLP. Step 1 loads the intermediate Parquet and validates that every row has a FILE_DATA_ID. Step 2 loads resources once, including a real-word vocabulary built from NLTK and WordNet and cached to disk, so later runs skip the rebuild. Cleaning, lemmatization and real-word filtering produce a valid-word count per document, and anything under 40 is flagged SUCCESSFULLY_PARSED=N but kept. Keyword extraction runs TF-IDF, KeyBERT in batches of 32 and LDA, then merges them. Steps 7 to 9 fit the output to the database: keyword strings truncated to 500 to 1,000 characters for column limits, and the output column schema enforced. Step 10 converts lists and dicts to JSON strings for Parquet and concatenates parsed and skipped rows. Step 11 builds the staging tables.

cards.title: Data quality checks at stage boundaries
questions: what data quality checks run between stages
do your stages write counts
how do you measure parse failures
parse status ok partial empty
coverage checks on a training corpus
how do you detect a partial join
health check output in cron logs
data quality metrics per document
how does she check data between pipeline steps
what do you log at each stage boundary
what numbers do you capture after each step
noticing that only a fraction of records matched a join
cards.answer: Every stage boundary writes counts, not just frames, because several defects I've caught were plausible output with the wrong number of rows behind it. The proposals run prints intermediate row counts, column counts, parse success rates and database confirmation counts, and saves per-document metadata such as document type, alpha ratio and content length to Parquet. The legislative join-key failure surfaced through row-count validation between stages. For LLM extraction I made parse_status (OK, PARTIAL, EMPTY) a first-class per-chunk column, so parse failures are counted instead of absorbed. Beyond counts, I check coverage against what should exist: a corpus with 1.2% passed-bill coverage was large and wrong. And a partial join is a failure signal, not a result; before the fix only about 8,820 of 50,501 bills matched, by numeric collision.

cards.title: Aligning a new state or source to an existing pipeline
questions: how would you add a new state to the legislative pipeline
schema alignment across sources
multi state config
what broke when you extended to california
state specific text cleaning
two tier taxonomy federal and state
onboarding a new data source
how does she generalize a pipeline to new sources
source specific procedural stage map
florida new york texas data
how is state specific logic kept apart from shared code
cards.answer: I make the source-specific parts configuration and the shared parts code, and I assume the new source breaks the definitions until I've checked. The legislative pipeline takes a multi-state config.json, and the taxonomy is two tiers: 42 universal federal categories plus a state layer, with Illinois adding 21 keyword augmentations and 5 state-only categories. California still needed its own procedural stage map, built from an iterative audit of unlabeled actions, and text cleaning added after the first run to strip journal page numbers and legislator names that dominated the features. The definition broke too: California's reached-vote target first captured committee votes, 80.4% of roll calls, which made it trivial; restricting it to floor votes fixed that. Florida, New York and Texas data is extracted with pipelines ready. Within Illinois, the trap was two ID spaces for one bill.

cards.title: Bronze, silver and gold layers in the legislative pipeline
questions: do you use a medallion architecture
bronze silver gold layers
how are the legislative pipeline layers organized
why isolate silver paths per profile
what lives in the gold layer
raw versus standardized data layers
layered data architecture
how does she structure pipeline layers
how are raw, cleaned and curated data separated
how did you stop evaluation runs overwriting each other
cards.answer: The legislative pipeline is layered Bronze, Silver, Gold: Bronze is ingested source, Silver is chunked text and LLM feature extraction, Gold is the standardized features the application reads. The layering earns its keep three ways. Isolation: during the model evaluation each configuration wrote to its own Silver paths, chunks_<profile> and features_<profile>, so no two grid cells shared state and the grid was reproducible. Recoverability: raw model output survives standardization, and keyword matching runs against the raw value first, so normalization never silently destroys a match. A clean publish boundary: Gold lives in Azure per session, with features, Explorer metadata, FAISS index and config verified before a session counts as done. Extraction happens once per bill upstream, while per-user scoring reads Gold, so adding a user never re-extracts the corpus.

cards.title: Running LLM extraction as a pipeline stage
questions: how do you treat an llm step inside a data pipeline
llm extraction as a pipeline stage
how do you make llm extraction restartable
parse status for llm output
pinning model versions in a pipeline
bounding llm input with chunking
data engineering around llm extraction
how does she productionize llm extraction in a pipeline
making a multi day llm batch job behave like etl
which model version produced the extracted features
llm responses that don't parse
cards.answer: I treat an LLM step like any other unreliable upstream: bounded input, typed output, counted failures and restartability. In the legislative pipeline, text is normalized and chunked before extraction, so a one-line amendment and a 400-page act arrive in the same shape. The model emits a 15-field structured schema parsed downstream, and each chunk carries parse_status as OK, PARTIAL or EMPTY, so parse failures are a measured rate instead of silent nulls. The extractor flushes in batches and can be killed and restarted without double-writing, which a roughly 155-hour run over 11,673 bills requires. Raw output is kept beside the standardized field. And I pin what produced it: evaluated model versions were recorded by blob digest. The research proposals pipeline keeps the LLM out for now; its semantic phase is scaffolded but not built.

iv-test-data-pipelines.answer: I test pipelines with data I fabricate, contracts I freeze and checks that run in production. For the RIMS manifest I committed a 50-row synthetic fixture covering every format class, status value, path flag, duplicate case, nested-archive depth and suspect date, plus a deliberately broken variant that trips each validation rule, so the suite runs with no drive, no Box access and no credentials. It caught NaN being truthy in Python, which had put every row in layer 0. The retirement rebuild validates its output against a frozen contract on every run, and a preflight script checks the Oracle client, credentials, imports, files and directory permissions before the first scheduled run. A float equality check that passed at 224 rows and failed at 225 became a tolerance with a printed drift. In production the checks are post-write row counts and magic-byte checks on inputs, and when I fixed train and serve skew I verified 36,028 inputs byte-identical.
